title: Money, services and complaints
cando: complain and get a result, then plan your next steps in English

about.text: In this lesson, something you bought is faulty, and you complain until you get a result. You say what other people did for you with have or get something done, and you read the small print before you buy. This lesson ends the nine-month course, so you also make a plan for learning English on your own.
goals: Complain on the phone, and ask for a refund, a replacement or compensation.
Say what somebody else did for you: I had it repaired.
Use the more…, the…: The sooner you complain, the better.
Read simple returns terms, and write a clear complaint email.
Make a learning plan for after the course, and present it.

chapters.title: Fourteen days
chapters.text:
This is the last lesson of Level 3, and the end of the nine-month course. It is about money, services and complaints.
In the conversation, Omar phones a shop. His washing machine is faulty. He had it repaired, but now it's leaking again.
Listen to how he complains. He is polite, but he is firm. I'd like to make a complaint. I'd like a refund.
The shop says no to a refund, because it's more than fourteen days since he bought it. So Omar asks for something else. Listen for what he gets in the end.
A good complaint is clear. Say what you bought, what went wrong, and what you want.

chapters.title: Have it done
chapters.text:
There are two grammar points.
First, have or get something done. Omar did not repair the machine himself. The engineer did. So he says: I had it repaired. Have, then the thing, then a past participle.
Listen to the difference. I repaired my car means I did the work. I had my car repaired means a mechanic did it.
Get is the same, but more informal. I need to get my hair cut.
Second, a pattern for two things that change together. The more you order, the lower the price. The sooner you complain, the better. Remember to say the in both halves.

chapters.title: The small print, and a plan
chapters.text:
In Section 3 you read two short texts.
The first is the small print from a shop: its rules for returns and repairs. Read it carefully. The numbers are important. How many days? How much?
The second is Priya's learning plan for the six months after her course.
Then you write two things. First, a complaint email: what you bought, what went wrong, what you had done, and what you want. Then your own learning plan.

chapters.title: Get a result, then plan ahead
chapters.text:
The real-life task has two parts.
First, you phone a shop about headphones that have stopped working again. Don't stop at the first no. Stay polite, say clearly what you want, and ask for it in writing.
Then you present your plan for learning after the course. Say your main aim. Then say your habit: a fixed time and place, not a number of hours. Twenty minutes on the bus every morning is better than an hour when you have time.
The nine-month course ends here, but your English doesn't. Keep going.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a longer story or article about money and services.
Read it once for the story. Did the people get a good result? What would you do in their place?
Then answer the questions, and tell Wehel about a time you complained.

warmup.prompt: Something you bought is faulty. What do you do first?
choices: take it back to the shop
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Many people phone first, then send an email so they have everything in writing. And always keep your receipt!

conversation.title: Fourteen days
conversation.setting: Omar bought a washing machine from Corvane Home, an online shop. He phones their customer service.
lines: Adviser
Thank you for holding. You're through to Corvane Home customer service. My name's Hannah. How can I help?
Omar
Hello. I'd like to make a complaint. I've been on hold for forty minutes.
Adviser
I'm very sorry about the wait. What's the problem?
Omar
I bought a washing machine from you in March. It was in the sale, so I thought it was a bargain. After three weeks it started leaking. I had it repaired by your engineer, but now it's leaking again.
Adviser
I'm sorry to hear that. Can I have your order number and the date of purchase?
Omar
It's four seven seven two, and I bought it on the second of March.
Adviser
Thank you. Would you like us to send the engineer again?
Omar
No, thank you. I don't want to get it repaired again. It's clearly faulty, and I'm fed up with it. I'd like a refund.
Adviser
I'm afraid we only give refunds for fourteen days from the date of purchase. After that, we can offer a repair or a replacement.
Omar
Then I'd like a replacement, please, and some compensation. I've been going to the launderette for two weeks, and the longer this goes on, the more it costs me.
Adviser
That's fair. We'll take the old machine back when we deliver the new one, and I can give you a thirty-pound voucher.
Omar
Thank you. When can you deliver it?
Adviser
This Friday, between eight and twelve. I'll send you an email to confirm.
Omar
Great. Thanks for your help, Hannah.

questions.q: What is wrong with Omar's washing machine?
questions.a: It is leaking again after a repair.
wrong: It was delivered to the wrong address.
questions.why: Omar says he had it repaired, but now it's leaking again.

questions.q: Why can't Omar get a refund?
questions.a: He bought it more than fourteen days ago.
wrong: He had it repaired by another company.
questions.why: The shop only gives refunds for fourteen days from the date of purchase.

questions.q: What does Omar get in the end?
questions.a: a new machine and a thirty-pound voucher
wrong: a refund and a new machine
a free repair and a refund
questions.why: Hannah says they will deliver a new machine and give him a thirty-pound voucher.

phrases.text: I'd like to make a complaint.
I had it repaired, but it's leaking again.
phrases.use: Saying you tried to fix the problem, and it didn't work.
Saying firmly that the product has a fault.

phrases.text: Then I'd like a replacement, please.
phrases.use: Asking for a new one when the first answer is no.
Asking for something extra, because the problem cost you time or money.

phrases.text: Can I have your order number?
phrases.use: What customer service often asks first. Have it ready.

phrases.text: I'll send you an email to confirm.

items.example: The kettle was faulty, so I took it back.

items.meaning: A new thing that you get instead of one that is broken or lost.
items.example: The shop gave me a replacement the same day.

items.meaning: Money or something else that you get because a problem cost you time, money or trouble.
items.example: The airline paid us compensation for the long delay.

items.meaning: A piece of paper or a code that you can use instead of money in a shop.
items.example: They gave me a twenty-pound voucher to say sorry.

items.meaning: Something you have bought, or the act of buying it.
items.example: Keep your receipt as proof of purchase.

items.meaning: To return something to the shop where you bought it; or, for a shop, to accept it back.
items.example: The shoes were too small, so I took them back.

items.meaning: Waiting on the phone until somebody can speak to you.
items.example: I was on hold for half an hour, listening to the same music.

items.meaning: Annoyed and unhappy about something that has gone on for too long.
items.example: I'm fed up with this slow internet.

items.meaning: Something you buy for much less than its usual price.
items.example: The coat was half price. What a bargain!

items.meaning: Something that costs money but is not worth it.
items.example: That cheap umbrella was a waste of money. It broke on the first day.

items.meaning: To have enough money to pay for something.

items.example: Thanks for lending me the money. I'll pay you back on Friday.

items.meaning: To keep money for some time, so that you can buy something later.
items.example: I'm saving up for a new laptop.

items.meaning: Money that you borrow, often from a bank, and pay back later.
items.example: They took out a loan to buy a van for the business.

items.meaning: All of it, not only part of it.
items.example: I paid the bill in full.

sound.title: I'd like, not I like
sound.explain: The d in I'd like is short, but it changes the meaning. I'd like means I want, and it is polite. I like means I enjoy. Join the d to like, with no gap. Listen, then say each pair.
lines: I'd like to make a complaint.
I'd like a refund, please.
Then I'd like a replacement, please.

sayIt.instructions: Say Omar's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Do you sound polite, but firm?
lines: Hello. I'd like to make a complaint. I've been on hold for forty minutes.
I had it repaired by your engineer, but now it's leaking again.
No, thank you. I don't want to get it repaired again. It's clearly faulty, and I'm fed up with it. I'd like a refund.
Then I'd like a replacement, please, and some compensation.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. In the first two, Omar talks about work that somebody else does. The last one puts two changes together.
examples: I had it repaired by your engineer.
I don't want to get it repaired again.
The longer this goes on, the more it costs me.
spot.question: Who repaired the machine: Omar, or somebody else? And in the last sentence, what happens to the cost as time goes on?
spot.answer: Somebody else repaired it: have or get + the thing + a past participle. The cost goes up: the longer…, the more… shows two things changing together, and both halves start with the.

rules.title: Have or get something done
rule: have + the thing + past participle: somebody else does the job for you.
I had my washing machine repaired. We're having the kitchen painted next week.
get means the same, and is more informal: I need to get my hair cut.
I repaired it = I did the work. I had it repaired = somebody did it for me.
Say who did it with by: I had it repaired by your engineer.
rules.mistake: Keep the order: have + thing + participle. Not: I had repaired my car at the garage. Say: I had my car repaired at the garage.

rules.title: The more…, the…
rule: the + comparative, the + comparative: two things change together.
The more you order, the lower the price.
The sooner you complain, the better. The longer you wait, the harder it gets.
Both halves start with the, and a comma goes between them.
The more you practise, the more confident you'll feel.
rules.mistake: Don't drop the second the. Not: The more you order, lower the price. Say: The more you order, the lower the price.

practice.q: My watch stopped, so I had the battery ___ .
practice.why: have + thing + past participle: had the battery changed.

practice.q: I didn't paint the flat myself. I ___ it painted.
practice.why: had + thing + participle means somebody else painted it.

practice.q: Your hair is very long! When are you going to get it ___ ?
practice.why: get + thing + past participle, and the participle of cut is cut.

practice.q: We're ___ a new boiler fitted next week.
practice.why: be having + thing + participle is for a job that is arranged.

practice.q: Which sentence means that a mechanic did the work?
practice.why: have + thing + participle means somebody else did it.

practice.q: The more you order, the ___ the price.
practice.why: Both halves use the + a comparative: the lower.

practice.q: The ___ you report a fault, the better.
The longer you leave it, ___ harder it gets.
practice.why: Both halves need the: the harder.

practice.q: The more you practise, the ___ you'll feel.
practice.why: A long adjective takes more: the more confident.

practice.q: I can't fix the washing machine myself. I need to get it ___ .
practice.why: get + thing + past participle: get it repaired.

yourTurn.prompt: Think of three jobs that somebody else did for you, or will do for you: at home, for your car, your phone or your hair. Write three sentences with have or get something done. Then write one sentence that starts with The more.
starters: Last month I had my … repaired.
yourTurn.model: Last month I had my phone screen replaced, because I dropped it on the bus. I had my flat painted last year, and it looks great. Next week I'm getting my eyes tested. The more I use my phone, the more often I have to charge it.

text.title: The small print, and a learning plan
text.type: Returns terms and a learning plan
text.body:
PRACTICE: Corvane Home is not a real shop.
CORVANE HOME: THE SMALL PRINT
Returns, repairs and payment
1. Changed your mind? Return unused goods in their box within 14 days of purchase for a full refund. Please include your receipt or invoice.
2. Faulty goods: tell us within 14 days of purchase, and we will give you a refund, a repair or a replacement.
3. After 14 days, we will repair faulty goods free of charge for 2 years. If we cannot repair them, we will replace them.
4. Please do not have our goods repaired by anybody else. If you do, your free repairs will end.
5. Paying monthly? We add a £12 charge to any overdue payment.
6. The more you spend, the more you save: 5% off orders over £500, and 10% off orders over £1,000.
This does not affect your legal rights.
---
MY LEARNING PLAN: THE NEXT SIX MONTHS
Priya Sharma. Written on 30 June. Next review: 31 December.
1. Where I am now: I have finished Level 3. My reading is good, but meetings are hard when people speak fast.
2. My main aim: to follow a team meeting at work without asking people to repeat things.
3. My habit: twenty minutes of listening on the bus, every weekday morning. A fixed time and place, not a number of hours.
4. Self-study: one short podcast a day. I will also revise my word lists every Sunday.
5. Checking my progress: I will record myself once a month and compare the recordings.
6. What might go wrong: I usually stop in August, when my routine changes. This year I will stick to my plan and keep going, even if it is only ten minutes a day.

gist.q: What does the first text tell customers?
gist.a: what happens if they return something or it needs a repair
wrong: how to use a washing machine safely
how to apply for a job at the shop
gist.why: It is the shop's small print about returns, repairs and payment.

gist.q: What is Priya's plan mainly about?
gist.why: Her main aim is to follow a team meeting at work without asking people to repeat things.

detail.q: Your fridge from Corvane Home stopped working five weeks after you bought it. What will the shop do?
detail.a: repair it free, or replace it if they can't repair it
detail.why: After 14 days, faulty goods are repaired free for 2 years, or replaced if they cannot be repaired.

detail.q: What happens if somebody else repairs your Corvane Home machine?
detail.why: If you have the goods repaired by anybody else, your free repairs will end.

detail.q: How much do you save on an order of £700?
detail.why: Orders over £500 get 5% off, and only orders over £1,000 get 10% off.

detail.q: How will Priya check her progress?
detail.a: She will record herself once a month.
wrong: She will take an exam in August.
Her teacher will test her every week.
detail.why: She says she will record herself once a month and compare the recordings.

items.meaning: The details of an agreement, often in small letters, that people forget to read.
items.example: Read the small print before you sign anything.

items.meaning: Things that are made to be sold.
items.example: The goods arrived two days late.

items.meaning: A document that lists what you bought or what work was done, and how much you must pay.
items.example: The builder sent us an invoice for £450.

items.meaning: Not paid, returned or done by the time it should be.
items.example: My phone bill is overdue, so I must pay it today.

items.meaning: Something that you want to achieve.
items.example: My aim is to speak confidently in meetings.

items.meaning: The process of getting better, or of moving closer to a goal.
items.example: I'm making good progress with my English.

items.meaning: To study something again so that you remember it.
items.example: I revise my new words every Sunday evening.

items.meaning: Something that you do regularly, often without thinking about it.
items.example: Reading the news in English every morning is a good habit.

items.meaning: Learning on your own, without a teacher.
items.example: I do an hour of self-study on the train.

items.meaning: To continue, even when it is difficult.
items.example: It's hard at first, but keep going.

items.meaning: To do what you planned or promised, and not change it.
items.example: If you stick to your plan, you'll see real progress.

model.title: A complaint email
model.body:
Subject: Faulty coffee machine, order 58190
Dear Corvane Home Customer Service,
I am writing to complain about a coffee machine that I bought from your website on 3 May. The order number is 58190, and I paid £129 in full.
After a week, the machine started leaking. I had it repaired by your engineer on 20 May, but the same problem has come back.
The machine is clearly faulty. I would like a replacement or a refund. I would also like some compensation for the two mornings I took off work to wait for the engineer.
I have attached my invoice and a photo of the leak. The sooner this is sorted out, the better. I look forward to hearing from you within seven days.
Kind regards,
Ana Costa

write.task: Write two things. First, a complaint email about something faulty, real or made up: what you bought and when, what went wrong, what you had done about it, and what you want. Then write your own learning plan for the six months after this course, with the six headings in Priya's plan.
write.starter: I am writing to complain about …
checklist: My email says what I bought, when, and what went wrong.
I used have or get something done, for example: I had it repaired.
I asked clearly for what I want: a refund, a replacement or compensation.
My plan has one main aim, and a habit with a time and a place.

card.title: Get a result, then plan ahead
card.situation: Three weeks ago you bought headphones from Vellmar Electronics for £80. You had them repaired at the shop last week, but they have stopped working again. Your English course is also ending, and your class wants to hear your plan for the next six months.
card.goal: Phone the shop, explain the problem and get a result: a refund or a replacement. Then follow up with a short email. Last, present your learning plan in one or two minutes.

phrases: I'd like to make a complaint, please.
I had them repaired, but they've stopped working again.
They're clearly faulty, so I'd like a refund or a replacement.
Could you put that in an email, please?
My main aim for the next six months is …
My habit will be … every … at …
prepare.notes: Before the call, write down what you bought, when, the price, the order number and what you want. For your plan, write one aim, one habit with a time and a place, and how you will check your progress.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher works for the shop. Phone and make your complaint, and don't give up until you get a result. Then present your learning plan to the class in one or two minutes.
doIt.wehel: You work in customer service at an electronics shop. I bought headphones for 80 pounds three weeks ago. You repaired them once, and now they have stopped working again. I will phone you to complain. First, offer only another repair. If I ask politely and clearly, offer a replacement. After the call, ask me about my plan for learning English after my course, and give me one useful tip. Use clear, simple English.

model.title: The call, and the plan
lines: Assistant
Good morning, Vellmar Electronics. How can I help?
You
Hello. I'd like to make a complaint, please. I bought some headphones from you three weeks ago.
Assistant
I'm sorry to hear there's a problem. What's wrong with them?
You
The sound keeps stopping. I had them repaired here last week, but now they've stopped working again.
Assistant
Oh dear. We can send them for repair again, if you like.
You
I'd rather not. They're clearly faulty. I paid eighty pounds in full, so I'd like a refund or a replacement, please.
Assistant
As this is the second fault, I can give you a replacement. You can collect it today.
You
That's fine. Could you put that in an email, please, so I have it in writing?
Assistant
Of course. I'll send it this afternoon.
You
Thank you. I'll bring the old pair in on Saturday.
Teacher
Well done. Now, what's your plan for learning after the course?
You
My main aim is to write better emails at work. My habit will be fifteen minutes of reading in my lunch break, every weekday.
Teacher
Good. And how will you check your progress?
You
Once a week, I'll ask a colleague to read one of my emails. And when work gets busy, I'll stick to my plan, even if it's only five minutes.
compare: Did you say what you bought, when, and what went wrong?
Did you say what you had done: I had them repaired…?
Did you ask clearly and politely for what you want, and get it in writing?
Did your plan have an aim, a habit with a time and a place, and a way to check your progress?

canDo: I can make a complaint on the phone, and ask for a refund, a replacement or compensation.
I can say what somebody else did for me with have or get something done.
I can read simple returns terms and understand what they mean for me.
I can write a clear complaint email.
I can make a learning plan with an aim, a habit and a way to check my progress.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first page. What do you think the people are buying, or complaining about?
reading.talk: Did the people in the story get a fair result? Have you ever complained about something you bought? What happened? Write three or four sentences, or tell Wehel.

quiz.q: I didn't fix my laptop myself. I had it ___ .
quiz.why: have + thing + past participle means somebody else did it.

quiz.q: We're getting the windows ___ next week.
quiz.why: get + thing + past participle: getting the windows cleaned.
Both halves need the: the sooner…, the better.

quiz.q: The shoes were half price. What a ___ !
quiz.why: A bargain costs much less than its usual price.

quiz.q: The kettle stopped working on the first day. It was ___ .
quiz.why: Faulty means it does not work properly.

quiz.q: Your phone bill is ___ . You should have paid it last week.
quiz.why: Overdue means not paid by the time it should be.

quiz.q: Which is the best habit for learning after the course?
options: twenty minutes of listening on the bus every morning
a lot of study when I have free time
one long weekend of study before a test
quiz.a: twenty minutes of listening on the bus every morning
quiz.why: A good habit has a time and a place, so it happens every day.

quiz.q: Your new machine ___ on Friday morning.
quiz.why: The machine does not deliver itself, so use the passive: will be delivered.

quiz.q: Something has come up, so we need to put the meeting ___ .
quiz.why: put off means move to a later time.

quiz.q: I left my umbrella on the train. I ___ been more careful.
quiz.why: should have means it didn't happen, and that was a mistake.

liveClass: Day 1: practise Omar's phone call in pairs, then change the product and the problem: a phone with a cracked screen, a jacket with a broken zip, a delivery that never arrived.
Day 2: have or get something done. Each learner says three jobs they have had done this year. Then each learner finishes this sentence in their own way: The more you practise, the …
Day 3: the real-life task. You work for the shop; each learner complains by phone and gets a result. Then each learner presents their learning plan in one or two minutes.
Day 4: talk about the book. Then look back at the course: each learner says one thing they can do in English now that they couldn't do at the start.
